findings.summary: The pin covers 3 of the 5 counted request kinds: `lists` and `deletes` are unconstrained. A per-stream LIST in `RemoteSequencer.commitAll` survives all 497 sequencer tests -- MEASURED. Round one closed this hole for PUT by name; the same hole is still open one kind over.
findings.detail: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED. `Cost` is built as `(gets + stats, puts)` at :154-155, so `StoreCounts.lists()` and `StoreCounts.deletes()` never reach an assertion. Inserted in `RemoteSequencer.commitAll`, after the lease read: `for (CommitRequest r : requests) { for (int i = 0; i < r.recordCounts().size(); i++) { store.list(leaseConfig.leaseKey(), null, 100); } }`. Result: `:sequencer:test` 497 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors -- `FleetSequencerCostTest` included. Probed the counter directly under that mutation: at 1/2/4 streams the deltas are `gets=2 stats=1 puts=1 lists=1/2/4`. That is a LIST per stream per forwarded flush -- forbidden three times over: non-negotiable 6 (a rate scaling with streams), cost.md R2 (never LIST on a hot path; a LIST costs 12.5 GETs) and R15 (LIST's own ~1/s ceiling). cost.md's own Enforcement section names `assertThat(stats.listRequests()).isZero()` as one of the three cost assertions to write FIRST, and this is the tree's first cost assertion on the forwarding path. The prose now claims more than the assertions deliver: the class javadoc at :19 says this file is 'What the forwarding path COSTS, in object-store requests' (all five kinds), and SPEC.md:305 now reads '+3 per follower commit, per-flush and PINNED (M5.33)'. The fix is additive and does not need a split: the fixture already holds `before` and `after`, so `after.lists() - before.lists()` and `after.deletes() - before.deletes()` are two `isZero()` lines at one and four streams, non-vacuous because the same fixture simultaneously asserts 3 reads and 1 write, proving the path ran. This is the same class-versus-instance miss the round-one PUT finding was: the reported instance was fixed, the class was not.
findings.failure_scenario: M5.6g rewrites `commitAll` to answer `tryLead()` from the lease the forwarder already read. Whoever writes it -- or any later change to that method, such as discovering a holder by scanning the lease prefix -- adds `store.list(...)` on the commit path. MEASURED: with a LIST issued once per `RunKey` in `commitAll`, the entire sequencer module stays green at 497/0, this test still reports 3 reads and 1 write, and SPEC.md:305 still says '+3 per follower commit ... PINNED'. A fleet flushing 500 streams per pod then pays 500 LISTs per forwarded flush -- at 12.5 GETs apiece the single most expensive request kind, and R15's ~1/s ceiling is breached by one pod -- with no gate, no test and no cost cell saying so.

findings.summary: "would have taken that file to 723 lines" does not reproduce -- MEASURED 751, and 754 once the three imports it would need are counted. The neighbouring 657 is right.
findings.detail: MEASURED by doing the merge: `head -n -1 FleetSequencerTest.java` (657 lines, last brace dropped) plus lines 64-158 of this file (the blank, the method javadoc, the method, the `Cost` record, `forwardedCommitCost`, the closing brace) gives 751 lines, and `FleetSequencerTest` imports none of `RunKey`, `LinkedHashMap` or `Map`, so the real figure is ~754. 723 is 66 lines of growth; the actual growth is 94. 723 looks like a figure computed against the ROUND-ONE version of this file, before the PUT paragraphs, the SIX-NOT-TWELVE paragraph and the two `writes()` assertions added ~28 lines to it -- i.e. a measured number that went stale inside its own commit, which is the defect class this task exists to correct and the one round one blocked on. The conclusion is unaffected: 751 and 723 are both over 700, so code-structure.md rule 1 forces the split either way. Either restate 751 or drop the arithmetic and say 'past 700'.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader auditing whether the split was forced re-does the arithmetic, gets 751 rather than 723, and cannot tell which of the two numbers in the same sentence to trust -- in a javadoc whose neighbouring paragraph rests its authority on 'MEASURED, not reasoned'. The 657 beside it is correct, so the cheap check (`wc -l`) passes and only the expensive one fails, which is the worst combination for a reader deciding how much of this file's prose to believe.

findings.summary: The round-one two-site hand-off was fixed in SPEC.md and re-created in this javadoc and in backlog.md:42, which now contradict SPEC.md:305's own four-site enumeration added by the same diff.
findings.detail: SPEC.md:305 now says 'when it lands FOUR sites change, not two: this cell, BOTH `isEqualTo(3L)` values, the test's own name, and the GET/STAT/GET breakdown in its javadoc' -- correct, and verified: this file holds exactly two `isEqualTo(3L)`, the count is in the method name (`...CostsTHREEReadsAndONEWrite...`) and the breakdown is at :69-72. But :100-103 of this same file says 'when that lands this assertion changes to 1 and the SPEC's cost row with it', and backlog.md:42's done cell says 'both the cell and the assertion change when it lands'. Both are the two-site framing round one flagged, now standing in the two places M5.6g's author is most likely to be reading -- the file being edited, and the row of the task that hands the work over. Only the assertion values are self-enforcing, which the SPEC says and these two do not.
findings.failure_scenario: M5.6g's author opens this file, follows the javadoc at :102, changes the two `isEqualTo(3L)` values to 1, and ships a test called `aForwardedCommitCostsTHREEReadsAndONEWriteAtANYNumberOfStreams` whose javadoc still spells out 'reads the lease (one GET) ... an election (a STAT and a GET)' while asserting one read -- the stale-prose defect M5.27, M5.32 and M5.34 each exist to clean up, recreated by the hand-off note inside the file it governs. SPEC.md:305 has the right enumeration, but nothing points the editor of this file at it.
